Country.evidence_source: In the Acholi culture roles are gendered, with men always regarded as the producer of wealth in the home and as the head of the family (El-Bushra & Sahl, 2005; Liu Institute for Global Issues, Gulu District NGO Forum & Ker Kwaro Acholi, 2005). Men are supposed to be in control of all the family resources, including children and wives. And for the rural men in Acholiland, land and livestock were the source of their wealth.

Area.evidence_source: These increasing aggressive tendencies toward their spouses seemed to have contributed to the suicides of some of the women in our study as expressed in the following voices: "Alcohol made him aggressive; whenever he drank he became violent toward his wife . . ." (case16:informant3). And "they were living peacefully until our father had a very sudden change in his character. He could drink too much, come back [home] late and fight her, such behavior took about three months . . . and she died." They would fight every evening (case18:informant3). To these women it had become more or less a routine to expect a fight and/or violent beating whenever their husbands went drinking. In the process injuries were sustained, and often the husband would target the very parts already injured, leading to chronic unbearable physical and psychological pain. Male drinking behavior in IDP camps has been implicated as a causal factor for many women's attempted suicide and suicidal deaths (Dolan, 2009). Similar to what Silberschmidt (2001) said of the men in Tanzania and Kenya, these men were probably using alcohol as a way of coping or exercising or restoring their masculinity. According to Möller-Leimkühler, aggression and alcohol are a "symbolic practice for demonstrating masculinity" (Möller-Leimkühler, 2003, p. 4). Alcohol intoxication is known to facilitate aggressive and impulsive behavior (Brady, 2006; Hufford, 2001; Sher, 2006; Tumwesigye & Kasirye, 2005). Conversely, disempowered men are said to have tendencies toward using aggression as a means to exert control over their wives (Silberschmidt, 2001). That way they could advertently drive their spouses to suicide. To other men, alcohol seemed to have facilitated revenge toward the deceased. For example, in one of our elderly decedents, suicide followed mistreatment by his son (see Kizza, Knizek, Kinyanda, & Hjelmeland, in press). The son first used to get drunk before he would go and terrorize the father, blaming him for having abandoned them [the children] when they were still very young and denying them a proper future. At times the son would even assault his father, as narrated by the informant below: The deceased though stayed with him [the son] but he did not live a very happy life. . . . he [son] would be aggressive toward mzee [the old man] . . . That son had been to the bush, so mzee was living in constant fear as he would act aggressively toward him and often talked about killing him . . . The son used to drink a lot so mzee at times could run away from home and spend some nights in the neighboring camp. (case8:informant2) The informant above implies that the decedent led an unhappy life while under the care of his son; that he was living in constant fear since whenever the son got drunk, he could get aggressive, assault him, and threaten to kill him. Unfortunately for the deceased, he hardly had anyone to turn to for help since the son was feared by others because of his past rebel history. Thus, the deceased was trapped amidst violence, humiliation, possibly guilt, and social isolation. In summary, for a significant number of the deceased – and indirectly for the women and an old man – alcohol in one way or another sent them on a direct trajectory toward the suicidal act.
